messages.author: 0d4085b4474fa32a
messages.subject: stan model that works with my data divided in 3, but not with the entire dataset
parts:
Dear Stan list

I'm working with a pretty complex hierarchical model (which I attach just in case). My question is how can it be that if I divide the data into 3 groups, the model works pretty fast (14 hours for each group) and successfully*(see below), but when I run the model with the entire dataset  (my data is 180 participants with 40 obs of reaction times and 40 choices taken between 1-4) it takes 5 times longer and it fails to converge: lots of divergent transitions, lots of transitions that exceeded the maximum treedepth, and the chains not mixing. And of course, I'd like to fit the entire dataset, so I'll be happy to get suggestions on how to proceed from here.

I also  simulated data and I recovered it successfully. I'm playing now with priors and I'm increasing the the max treedepth and the adapt alpha. Now I'm trying this model with adapt_delta=.999,max_treedepth=14,stepsize=0.01, and it's taking already 10 days (I've run the 3 groups of the data with these settings in 2 days in total!, but I also ran small subsets with less adapt_delta and max_treedepth and they worked).



I'm using rStan 2.9,  sorry for the old syntax in the file.


I said successfully* because the entire code runs, but at the end I get this:

> proc.time()
      user     system    elapsed 
   160.743      7.937 148188.417 

 *** caught segfault ***
address 0x7f39f27e15a8, cause 'memory not mapped'

Traceback:
 1: .Call(list(name = "CppObject__finalize", address = <pointer: 0x33b57a0>,     dll = list(name = "Rcpp", path = "/usr/local/lib/R/site-library/Rcpp/libs/Rcpp.so",         dynamicLookup = TRUE, handle = <pointer: 0x2d00100>,         info = <pointer: 0x7f39fe895dc0>), numParameters = 2L),     <pointer: 0x2fbf19a0>, .pointer)
 2: x$.self$finalize()
 3: (function (x) x$.self$finalize())(<environment>)
An irrecoverable exception occurred. R is aborting now ...
Segmentation fault (core dumped)


Thanks,
Bruno

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: stan model that works with my data divided in 3, but not with the entire dataset
parts:
On Thursday, August 18, 2016 at 11:00:35 AM UTC-4, Bruno Nicenboim wrote:
I'm using rStan 2.9,  sorry for the old syntax in the file.


I said successfully* because the entire code runs, but at the end I get this:

Don't use 2.9.x because it segfaults when R is closed in some Linux environments. Don't use 2.10.x because it is wrong. Use 2.11.x.

Your model is a bit too complicated to immediately recognize why it is not working well. You can improve the speed a bit by not calling sampling statements within a loop over the observations; just collect the likelihood contributions in a vector inside the loop and do
target += likelihood_contributions;
outside the loop. But that won't change the shape of your posterior distribution, which is where the real problem lies somewhere.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: stan model that works with my data divided in 3, but not with the entire dataset
parts:
With more data, the posterior can be more highly curved
(same phenomenon as narrowing posterior intervals) and
harder to move through with the Hamiltonian simulation.

The usual advice applies, which is to try a higher adapt_delta,
and if that doesn't work, reparameterize.

It can help immensely to put everything on a unit scale.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: stan model that works with my data divided in 3, but not with the entire dataset
parts:
> On Aug 18, 2016, at 10:32 PM, Bruno Nicenboim <bruno.n...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> thanks for all the answers:
>
> @Ben: I would like to avoid for now installing a new version, I'm running the models in a server, and there are other people using Stan right now. Do you think that "target += likelihood_contributions;" will be critical?
That's just new syntax for "increment_log_prob(likelihood contributions)".

>
>
> @Krzysztof: what do you mean by look at model vs. data comparisons? And the thing is that I don't want to start modifying the model, I don't mind if the the model has a terrible fit to the data (in fact I'll be even happy if this is the case). But I guess I can't argue that the model doesn't fit the data well just by the lack of convergence, right?
>
> @Bob: I parametrized everything as best I could do following the advice of the stan-list, and I put everything that I could in unit scale.
>
>
> And another general question is, can I use the 3 estimates of the parameters that I have from the 3 subsets of the data as initial values for fitting the complete dataset? Is this a good idea?

Maybe. Are the chains all getting to roughly the same place
and converging to the same adaptation parameters (mass matrix
and step size)? If so, starting near or in the typical set will
help speed up adaptation because it won't have to find the typical set.

Or are they getting stuck in weird places? That's a sign of
bigger trouble as Michael keeps pointing out on our lists.

Have you already increased adapt_delta and decreased stepsize?

You just want to be careful to add some noise so that you can
measure convergence.
> Or can I use the average of the 3 estimates for the priors of the model that I'll fit to the whole dataset?

This is the focus of a lot of work on parallelizing MCMC. The
problem is that the effect of the prior is going to change. But
it should be OK for inits.

- Bob

@krzysztof: A brief explanation about the model

The idea of the model is that participants take the same time (mu_rt) to make any of the 4 decisions (stored as winner) and this time is independent of the experimental manipulation (but it varies by participant and by item, the so-called random effects). The experimental manipulation affects the decision (winner[i]), also with random effects by participant and by item, but not the time. The complicated thing about the model, is that when a participant makes a wrong decision (!=1) then there's a probability  P_redo of redoing the decision and getting it right, and when that happens the time is increased (in log scale) by mu_add. The final time is log-normal distributed but shifted by participants. Maybe I'm skipping some details, but it seems to be identified and I can recover roughly the parameters.

I'm attaching a simplified version which is non-hierarchical and with a non-shifted distribution, and the code in R that generates data.

@Bob: I couldn't check if chains converged to the same adaptation parameters (I only saved the printed output), so I'll check it with the next model that finishes. And I want to try another model with init values anyway in the meanwhile, what does it mean to add some noise to measure convergence?, is something like 1 SD enough? too much? too little?

@Ben: I tried to do the increment_log_prob(likelihood contributions) with the much simpler non-hierarchical version of my model, and it took slightly longer. Is this something that should have some benefit only in very complex models? Should I try it anyway?

> The experimental manipulation affects the decision (winner[i]), also with random effects by participant and by item, but not the time.

So I wouldn't say that's independent of the manipulation if
the manipulation affects random effects and those effect

time.

> The complicated thing about the model, is that when a participant makes a wrong decision (!=1) then there's a probability P_redo of redoing the decision and getting it right, and when that happens the time is increased (in log scale) by mu_add. The final time is log-normal distributed but shifted by participants. Maybe I'm skipping some details, but it seems to be identified and I can recover roughly the parameters.

That sounds like a reasonable model at this level. Can they also
redo it and go from right to wrong or is it one way?

> I'm attaching a simplified version which is non-hierarchical and with a non-shifted distribution, and the code in R that generates data.
>
> @Bob: I couldn't check if chains converged to the same adaptation parameters (I only saved the printed output), so I'll check it with the next model that finishes.

Looks like retrieving the mass matrix is broken in RStan 2.11. We'll
fix it for the next release (may be a patch or 2.12). But you can look
at step sizes and tree depth.
> And I want to try another model with init values anyway in the meanwhile, what does it mean to add some noise to measure convergence?, is something like 1 SD enough? too much? too little?

By default, Stan initializes all parameters uniformly in (-2, 2) on
the unconstrained scale (then, e.g, positive parameters are exp
transformed, bounded parameters are inv_logit transformed, etc.).

We want to start in different parts of the posterior to find different
modes and make sure each chain is able to move to the same posterior
volume and mix there. You can see the description of R-hat in
the manual or in Gelman's books or papers. So we'd recommend initializing
around a single point, even if you start there.

- Bob
